options.label: A
options.text: Prose rules only: step 2 weighs an import's direction, shared code moves down to the lowest package both callers may import, and a function-local import placed to dodge a cycle is a defect fixed by moving the code. Cost: a written constraint with no check, against the cheatsheet's rule that every constraint has one.

options.label: B
options.text: Prose rules plus a suite lint check: the project declares its layer order in ok-planner's configuration, and a new check in the suite's lint fails an import against it. Cost: per-language import parsing in a lint that today reads comments and compose files, a new configuration key with its config check and true-up offer, and an amendment to [decision:project-chooses-its-lint-checks](.ok-planner/design/decisions/project-chooses-its-lint-checks.md).

options.label: C
options.text: Prose rules plus a project-checked layering rule, after the stack-ports precedent: the suite states the rules, and a project with more than one package declares its layer order and checks it with an import linter for its language. Cost: a project that wires no such linter gets the text alone, and the suite cannot check the wiring.

options.label: D
options.text: Leave layering to each project's subjects and practices. Cost: the reuse rule keeps sending agents across package boundaries until an owner writes a practice, and every project words the rule its own way.

problem:
Plumbline's reuse rule tells an agent to import an existing function from wherever it sits, and no Plumbline rule says where shared code lives or which way an import may point. In a project with several packages, agents who follow the rule build import cycles between packages, so no package can be maintained on its own. The cheatsheet commits the suite to "Strict DRY: semantically identical logic lives in ONE place" and to "Every written constraint needs a check that fails on violation: layering → dependency lint", but no rule tells a project to declare its layers, so no project has a layering to lint.

The mechanism: section 6 of [plumbline-coding.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/docs/plumbline-coding.md#L66-L72), "Import, never copy", says in step 1 "Where it exists, import it", and in step 2 "Where a dependency-split rule seems to block the import, read what the module actually imports before assuming." Step 1 sends the agent to the function's current home. Step 2 weighs how heavy an import is and never which way it points. Each reuse can add an edge up or across the package graph, and nothing mechanical refuses a cycle: the suite's lint runs five checks, comment hygiene, citation resolution, no tests, compose ports, and compose labels ([plumbline:LINT_CHECK_NAMES](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/plumbline#L187)), and none reads imports. Where Python refuses a circular import at load time, an agent moves the import inside a function to get past the error instead of moving the shared code down.

The owner reports the harm from the LineScout platform (package `gridiq`), which runs Ruff and declares no layers: one import cycle of 12 units spanning its main services, three two-unit cycles, 13 imports of the project's own modules placed inside functions, two of them on the big cycle to dodge circular-import errors, and 12 of the 79 root modules, which act as the shared base, importing service packages. Each import was reasonable inside its task; together they keep the owner from splitting the platform into independently maintained parts. That evidence lies outside this tree.

The owner asks for rules that cover at least: the project declares its layer order and a lint fails an import that breaks it; before importing from a sibling or higher package, the agent moves the code down to the lowest package both callers may import; an import placed inside a function to dodge a circular-import error is a defect fixed by moving the code; and step 2 weighs an import's direction, not only its weight. The canonical rule files and the lint are this project's shipped product, so the change is the project's own, and the copies under `.claude/rules/` follow on the next `/ok`. Every line added to the rules costs context in every session, since [concept:cheatsheet](.ok-planner/design/concepts/cheatsheet.md) keeps that layer small. [decision:stack-ports-checked-as-a-suite-rule](.ok-planner/design/decisions/stack-ports-checked-as-a-suite-rule.md) is the precedent for a suite rule a project checks with the suite's lint where it applies, with a project lint, or with both. No corpus artifact speaks to import direction or layering.

The ruling decides what the suite prescribes about where shared code lives and how a project checks import direction.

recommendation.text:
State the layering rules in the suite and have each project check them with its own import linter. Step 2 of the reuse rule weighs an import's direction as well as its weight. Shared code lives in the lowest package every caller may import, and an agent moves a function down before importing it from a sibling or higher package. An import placed inside a function to dodge a circular-import error is a defect, fixed by moving the code. A project with more than one package declares its layer order and checks it with an import linter for its language. Record the rule as a suite decision beside the one for stack ports.

Rationale: this follows the stack-ports precedent, where the suite states a rule that holds for every project and lets a project check it with a lint that reads its own formats, which import graphs are: every language parses imports its own way, and mature import linters already exist for the common ones. It gives the cheatsheet's "layering → dependency lint" a layering to check, which prose alone (A) does not, and it costs a few lines of rules text where a suite check (B) costs a per-language import parser, a configuration key, and an offer. Leaving it to practices (D) leaves in place the rule that sends agents across packages, which is the harm reported. The flip case: if owners commonly run multi-package projects with no import linter wired, the rule stays text there, and a suite check (B) earns its parser, starting with the languages the suite's own users ship.

title: Plumbline says to import shared code but never where it lives, so agents build import cycles

options.label: A
options.text: The collision is a stack defect (the code now): the corpus says the owner repairs it by choosing another run-tag variable, and true-up's config offer refuses a port rename. Cost: an owner who would rather rename the port edits the config by hand.

options.label: B
options.text: The collision is a ports defect: the defect text opens with `ports` again, the owner repairs it by renaming the port, and the offer refuses a run-tag variable change. Cost: the rename reaches every compose file and command that reads the port variable, which the offer cannot edit.

options.label: C
options.text: The collision belongs to both keys: true-up's config offer accepts a draft that changes either the run-tag variable or the port name. Cost: the one defect whose offer names two keys, a special case beside the rule that a defect's first word names its key.

problem:
When `.ok-planner/config.json` declares a port name that is also `stack.tag_variable`, the variable the stack tool sets to the run tag, true-up's config offer accepts only a draft that changes the `stack` key and refuses a draft that renames the port. No corpus artifact says which of the two names the owner repairs, and [story:true-up-project-estate](.ok-planner/design/stories/true-up-project-estate.md) owes the owner that upgrading the suite never costs them work they wrote.

The mechanism: `plumbline config-check` and `stack up` print the same defect, 'stack.tag_variable "<NAME>" is also a name ports declares, and the stack tool sets it to the run tag', from [plumbline:stackDefects](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/plumbline#L297-L324) and [stack:stack_defects](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/stack#L288-L321). True-up's [true-up:config_named_keys](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L2778-L2779) names each config key whose name opens a defect's text, and [true-up:changed_keys](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L2782-L2793) refuses a draft that changes any key not named, as [`admin/ADMINISTRATION.md`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L122) says of the `config` offer. So the first word of the defect text alone picks the key the owner may change: the text opens with `stack`, and a port rename is refused as 'ports (changed)'. The offer edits `.ok-planner/config.json` alone. The `stack` key holds the start command that reads the run-tag variable, so a draft can rename the variable and the start command's use of it in one key. A port name is read by the project's compose files and commands, which the offer does not touch, so a port rename inside the config alone leaves them reading the old name.

The state of play: before sprint certification of `2026-10-14-stack-lifecycle` (run converge-2026-10-15T011914), the text opened with 'ports', so the offer accepted only a port rename. The run's defect i16 re-worded it to open with `stack` and recorded the choice as question call i29, reasoning that a port rename reaches every compose file and command that reads the port variable, while the start command reads the run-tag variable. [decision:stack-ports-checked-as-a-suite-rule](.ok-planner/design/decisions/stack-ports-checked-as-a-suite-rule.md) binds each published host port to a declared port name and says nothing of the run-tag variable.

The ruling decides which name true-up's config offer lets the owner change when the two collide.

recommendation.text:
Keep the collision a stack defect: the owner repairs it by choosing another run-tag variable, and true-up's config offer refuses a port rename for it. Record in the corpus, beside the rule that binds host ports to declared port names, that the run-tag variable may not be a declared port name and that the variable is what yields.

Rationale: the config offer edits only the project's configuration, and the run-tag variable and the start command that reads it both live in one key there, so the offer can make the whole repair without touching a file the owner wrote elsewhere. A port rename (B) leaves every compose file and command that reads the port on the old name, which the compose port check then flags, so the offer would hand the owner the work the true-up story says an upgrade never costs. Accepting both keys (C) adds a special case to a rule that now has none, for a repair whose cheaper side is known. The flip case: if projects' compose files commonly read the run-tag variable too, such as for image tags, a variable rename reaches as many files as a port rename, and only the owner knows which is cheaper, so both keys (C) earns its special case.

title: When a port name equals the run-tag variable, true-up's config offer lets the owner repair only the run-tag variable

options.label: A
options.text: The start-time answer decides (the code now): the corpus says a run whose daemon answered neither before its start command nor at `down` made no docker object. Cost: a start command that starts and later loses the daemon leaves labelled objects with no record.

options.label: B
options.text: Any answer the tool observes decides: the stack tool also probes the daemon after the start command exits, whether the start passed or failed, and `down` skips docker only where none of its probes answered. Cost: one more docker call on every `stack up`, and a daemon started and stopped inside the start command, or started by a later verification step, still escapes.

options.label: C
options.text: The answer at `down` alone decides: `down` skips docker whenever the daemon does not answer, and deletes the entry. Cost: a run known to have made labelled objects loses its entry while the daemon is stopped, and nothing later removes those objects.

options.label: D
options.text: An unreachable daemon leaves a docker-pending entry: `down` stops the process group, deletes the folder, and releases the ports, but keeps the entry marked as owing a docker removal, which a later cleanup performs once the daemon answers. Cost: on a machine where docker is installed and never started, a pending entry stays for every run and the registry listing grows without bound.

problem:
The stack tool's `down` skips every docker removal for a run whose docker daemon did not answer when `stack up` opened the run and does not answer at `down`, and then deletes the run's registry entry. A start command that starts the daemon, makes objects that carry the run's label, and has the daemon stop before `down` leaves those objects on disk with no entry that records them. [story:verification-leaves-no-artifacts-behind](.ok-planner/design/stories/verification-leaves-no-artifacts-behind.md) owes the owner that a run's artifacts are removed once it is over, and [decision:run-artifacts-recorded-by-the-stack-tool](.ok-planner/design/decisions/run-artifacts-recorded-by-the-stack-tool.md) says `down` removes every container, image, volume, and network that carries the label. Neither says what counts as a removal when the tool cannot reach docker.

The mechanism: [stack:start_run](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/stack#L723) probes the daemon once with `docker version`, before it runs the start command, through [stack:docker_reached](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/stack#L581-L589), and records the answer on the entry. At `down`, [stack:removal_steps](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/stack#L638-L653) asks [stack:docker_out_of_reach](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/stack#L592-L593) whether the recorded answer was no and a fresh probe also fails; where both hold, it reports that the daemon answered neither when the run started nor now, returns no docker refusal, and `down` deletes the entry. The periodic cleanup's [stack:in_use](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/stack#L816-L837) skips its running-container check on the same test. Where the start-time probe answered, `down` tries every docker removal, and a refused removal keeps the entry for a later cleanup, as [decision:run-artifacts-removed-with-the-run](.ok-planner/design/decisions/run-artifacts-removed-with-the-run.md) requires.

The state of play: sprint certification of `2026-10-14-stack-lifecycle` (run converge-2026-10-15T011914) added the skip as defect i17. Before it, a run that made no docker object, taken down on a machine with Docker Desktop installed and stopped, kept its entry and its leased ports behind four docker refusals, and every later cleanup refused it again. The skip fixes that machine. The gap is a run whose daemon came up after the start-time probe: the tool never learns the daemon answered, so a later stopped daemon reads as proof that the run made nothing. [decision:stack-tool-runs-each-run](.ok-planner/design/decisions/stack-tool-runs-each-run.md) says `down` deletes the entry once every removal succeeds, and does not say whether a skipped removal counts as one.

The ruling decides what evidence lets the stack tool conclude that a run made no docker object.

recommendation.text:
Count every daemon answer the stack tool observes. The tool probes the daemon before and after the start command, on a failed start as on a passing one, and records that the run reached docker where either probe answered. `down` and the cleanup skip docker only for a run that recorded no answer and whose daemon does not answer at `down`; a run that reached docker keeps today's rule, where a refused removal keeps the entry for a later cleanup.

Rationale: this keeps the i17 fix, since a run on a machine whose daemon never answered still ends with its entry deleted and its ports released, and it closes the observable form of the gap for one fast call per run. The start-time answer alone (A) treats an unobserved daemon as proof of nothing made, which the label decision's aim of removing exactly what a run made does not allow where one more probe would tell. The `down` answer alone (C) discards the record of a run the tool knows reached docker, against the removal decision's rule that a refused removal keeps the entry. A docker-pending entry (D) keeps the most evidence, but it rebuilds i17's harm as a registry that grows on every run of a machine with docker stopped. The flip case: if verification paths start the daemon after the start command, such as a drive whose later step builds labelled images, the after-start probe still misses them, and the docker-pending entry becomes worth its growing registry.

title: The stack tool decides a run made no docker object from one probe taken before the start command runs

options.label: A
options.text: Two administration files mark a payload copy (the code now): any folder holding a family's true-up core and administration document is a payload copy, and none of its files counts as a caller. Cost: a project file below such a folder that calls a retired script is never flagged, and true-up removes the copy it calls.

options.label: B
options.text: Only the payload that runs true-up is skipped: every other copy in the project counts as a caller. Cost: the suite's own repository gets a caller issue for each retired script its payload documents, and keeps each retired copy until the owner answers.

options.label: C
options.text: The project declares its payload copies in its configuration, and true-up skips the declared folders alone. Cost: a configuration key only the suite's own repository uses, with its config check and config offer to extend.

options.label: D
options.text: A file below such a folder is skipped only where the running payload carries a file at the same path relative to its own root, so a project file the payload does not carry still counts as a caller. Cost: a file the working tree's payload adds before the installed release carries it draws a caller issue, and holds its retired copy, until the next release.

problem:
True-up never counts a file as a caller of a retired suite script where the file sits below any folder in the project that holds both `admin/true-up` and `admin/ADMINISTRATION.md`, so it removes the retired copy even where such a file still calls it. [decision:retired-script-repoint-needs-a-proven-root](.ok-planner/design/decisions/retired-script-repoint-needs-a-proven-root.md) holds a retired copy wherever true-up cannot prove a line does not call it, because removing the copy can break a real caller while holding it costs only a kept file. [story:true-up-project-estate](.ok-planner/design/stories/true-up-project-estate.md) owes the owner that upgrading never costs them work they wrote.

The mechanism: true-up finds callers of a retired script with `git grep -F` over the tracked files, repoints what it can, files an intake issue for each file it cannot repoint, and keeps the retired copy while such an issue names it. [true-up:caller_kind](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L1912-L1930) returns no caller for a file that [true-up:payload_copy_file](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L1903-L1909) places below a folder holding the two administration files, and the skip clause in [admin/ADMINISTRATION.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L247) says the same. Two file names alone mark the folder; nothing checks that a file below it belongs to a payload.

The state of play: sprint certification of `2026-10-14-stack-lifecycle` (run converge-2026-10-15T011914) added the skip as defect i19. In the suite's own repository, `/ok` runs the installed payload from the plugin cache, so the payload copy in the tree is not the payload that runs true-up. Before the fix, that copy's own documentation of the retired `.ok-planner/bin/run-tag` and `.ok-planner/bin/port-block` drew caller issues and kept both retired copies for good. The fixer recorded the choice as question call i31 and rejected matching a file's content against the running payload, which fails once the working tree moves past the installed release. Only the suite's own repository is known to carry a payload copy in its tree.

The ruling decides what proves a file is part of a family payload copy that true-up does not search for callers.

recommendation.text:
Skip a file below a folder holding the two administration files only where the payload that runs true-up carries a file at the same path relative to its root. Every other file below such a folder counts as a caller, as any project file does.

Rationale: the retired-script decision lets true-up drop a caller only on proof, and holds the copy where it cannot tell, because a kept file is the cheap side of the error. A path the running payload also carries is that proof, and it survives the working tree moving past the installed release, which the content match the fixer rejected does not. Its one false positive is a payload file newer than the installed release, which costs a kept copy and an issue until the next release: the cost the decision already accepts. The two-file mark (A) removes a copy a real caller may still need, the harm the decision names. Skipping only the running payload (B) leaves the suite's own repository with standing false issues on every run. A declared folder (C) adds a configuration key that one repository uses, and still trusts the whole folder. The flip case: if the suite's own repository routinely adds payload files that document retired scripts ahead of a release, the false issues recur each release, and a declared folder (C) earns its key.

title: True-up treats any folder holding two administration files as a payload copy, and removes a retired script a file below it still calls
